creator: elemental.math
caption:
Can one line of math build an entire 3D world? This is the Mandelbulb, and it comes from z ↦ z⁸ + c.

In 2D, the Mandelbrot set repeats z ↦ z² + c: pick a point c, start at zero, square, add c, repeat. If it never escapes past |z| = 2, the point is black. Squaring a complex number squares its length and doubles its angle.

There is no such multiplication for points in 3D. William Rowan Hamilton tried for years; in an 1865 letter he remembers his sons asking every morning, "Well, Papa, can you multiply triplets?" and his answer, "No, I can only add and subtract them." Daniel White's 2007 idea was to copy the geometry in spherical coordinates, and Paul Nylander raised it to the 8th power: r ↦ r⁸, θ ↦ 8θ, φ ↦ 8φ, then add c.

To draw it, every pixel shoots a ray. The formula gives a distance the ray can safely jump, d = ½ · r · log r / dr, and the ray jumps that far and asks again. The ray in the video needed 13 jumps (1.507, 0.219, 0.090 … 0.0009).

One frame of this video, counted pixel by pixel: 8,294,400 rays, 102,780,876 jumps and 307,247,022 turns of the formula (1080 × 1920, 4 rays per pixel, 15 iterations).

The formula, the distance estimate and the ray-marching loop are ported line by line from Mandelbulber's source (GPL-3.0, commit 109fd69): github.com/buddhi1980/mandelbulber2
Hamilton's letter (5 Aug 1865): maths.tcd.ie/pub/HistMath/People/Hamilton/Letters/BroomeBridge.html
Daniel White on the Mandelbulb: skytopia.com/project/fractal/mandelbulb.html

#math #fractals #mandelbulb #computergraphics #creativecoding
transcript: This one line of math builds an entire world. It runs inside Mandelbulb, an open source program that flies a camera through fractals. It all starts flat, with the Mandelbrot set. Pick a point C, start at zero, square it, add C, and repeat. If it never runs away, paint it black. And squaring hides a trick. The length gets squared, and the angle doubles. In three dimensions, numbers like that do not exist. William Hamilton spent years trying to multiply triplets. Every morning his sons asked, well Papa, can you multiply triplets? And he always answered, no, I can only add and subtract them. So Daniel White just copied the geometry, and Paul Milander pushed it further. Raise the length to the eighth power, and multiply both angles by eight. At power two, it's a lumpy blob. At power eight, it blooms, with bumps on bumps all the way down. To draw it, every pixel shoots a ray. The formula says how close the surface could be. So the ray jumps exactly that far, and asks again. This one needed thirteen jumps. One frame of this video takes eight million rays, a hundred million jumps, and three hundred million turns of that one line. And all of it comes from one line.

creator: thewallstreetskinny
caption:
In case you missed it, there’s been turmoil in AI stocks, sparked by concern over Coreweave’s debt. Here’s exactly what you need to know about the neoclouds.

A few things I couldn’t fit in the video time limit of 3 min: 

1. The advance rate, meaning how much neoclouds can borrow relative to the amount of money they need to spend on Capex (to buy chips and equipment) can get QUITE high, in some cases 90-95%+ depending on the credit of the “off-taker”, so from Meta for example. 

2. Asset backed financing and project financing (one of the groups I worked in at Morgan Stanley) isn’t new. What is unique about these GPU backed financings are the much shorter contract length; in the power world you often see power purchase agreements of 15-20 years and assets that have a much longer useful life (think a gas turbine). In a power deal, the debt is shorter than the PPA, and the PPA is shorter than the asset’s life, which leaves a long tail. Here the loan, the contract, and the asset useful life are much closer in length, so there is a shorter tail behind the debt. 

Now in fairness to the neoclouds, after the off-taker's contracts end the same GPUs can be rented on an hourly basis at higher rates (at least right now) because demand for compute is so high.

While Coreweave does have other types of debt, this structure accounts for over half and funded much of its massive growth over the past few years. They also have a decent amount of convertible debt, which is typically utilized by higher risk companies. 

A huge reason for the stock sell off though was the corporate debt yields blew out to 15% (tweeted about by Chamath Palihapitiya to which Elon responded “yikes”), which spooked the market.

3. And finally what surprised me was the fact that on the other side, so if you look at an Anthropic’s balance sheet, “take or pay” agreements to buy the compute do not show up as a liability on the balance sheet, rather just shown as a footnote!!While this is consistent with accounting rules, it’s surprising.
transcript: we need to talk about what's going on with CoreWeave. It plunged 15% and is taking a bunch of the other AI stocks down with it. I happened to work in CDO structuring at Morgan Stanley in 2008. I'm going to explain exactly what's going on in under three minutes. Let's begin with where we are within the AI ecosystem. We're in layer three, the infrastructure, which at its core can be thought of as the companies who sell compute. Now compute is the raw processing power needed to train AI models. And Wall Street splits those companies into two categories. First there are the hyperscalers, household names like Amazon's AWS or Microsoft's Azure. And second is the neoclouds, where the poster children are CoreWeave and Nebius. To understand the neocloud business, let's run through what NVIDIA CEO Jensen Wong calls an AI factory. First you need energy, second you need chips, and third you need the building or powered shell. Many of these neoclouds started as crypto miners, but pivoted their business when they realized AI was a better opportunity. The output of the AI factory is compute, but companies make money in different ways. Applied digital and core scientific are landlords. They own the powered shells and make money renting the real estate without taking on the risk of buying the chips. Of the companies that sell compute, vertically integrated players like Iran own their own powered shells. Crusoe got there from the other direction. It started with power generation and then built from there. But on the other hand, CoreWeave, Nebius, and Lambda historically didn't own the power or the buildings. And unlike the hyperscalers, they don't have any wildly profitable business throwing off cash flows either. Which brings us to a key difference between hyperscalers and neoclouds. Hyperscalers have an actual business beyond compute. Microsoft sells Office, Amazon is the everything store, and Google and Meta sell ads. These earnings then translate into real cash flows that Alisa first was able to fund AI CapEx. Recently though, CapEx has gotten so high that the hyperscalers have started raising debt. But when banks land at the corporate level, they look at leverage, or debt EBITDA. And against their huge earnings, the borrowing is still modest. Neoclouds, by contrast, need money to buy the chips. But they have two problems. First, they don't have the cash flows from another business to pay for them outright. And second, their existing businesses often can't support the amount of debt they need to fund the chips. What they do have, however, are valuable contracts with big players like Meta. Enter chipback financing. Borrow against the contract and the chips themselves. Put the contract and chips into an SPV and raise debt off the cash flows. For example, say CoreWeave signs a five-year contract with Meta for $100 million a year. Lenders ship out the expenses like rent and energy and size the debt. What's amazing for CoreWeave is they can borrow at much lower rates because lenders look at Meta's credit, not theirs. CoreWeave gets the cash, buys the chips, and voila, they sell compute. While this might seem great, the depreciation and interest eat away at much of the profit. But that's just one contract and one SPV. In reality, there are many. Customers like OpenAI and Anthropic need their businesses to keep growing to make payments. And the contracts are short. Unlike a 15-year agreement in the power industry, some are in just three years. Not to mention, the assets backing the debt, the chips, have relatively short useful lives. That's where NVIDIA comes in. CoreWeave is a major customer for NVIDIA's AI chips, so NVIDIA has a huge incentive for it to succeed, not to mention its 11% ownership stake. On top of that, NVIDIA has agreed to buy any compute capacity CoreWeave can sell, which helps lower borrowing costs. It's one of the many reasons the economists called NVIDIA the central bank of AI.
